title: Rublev's Trinity
hookLine: three angels at Abraham's table, with an open place at the table

lines: THREE FIGURES AT A LOW TABLE.
cards: Three figures sit around a low table. They have wings and long thin staffs, and their heads lean gently toward one another, as if in a quiet conversation. In the center of the table is a single cup.
Behind them, a house, a tree, a rock. The colors are soft: gold, deep blue, pale green. Nobody is eating or in a hurry.

And at the front of the table, the side nearest you, there's a gap. Room for one more. Tradition says this icon was painted by a monk named Andrei Rublev, for the monastery that grew up around Sergius.

teach.b: The scene comes from Genesis. Abraham sits at the door of his tent in the heat of the day, and in the King James Bible: "he lift up his eyes and looked, and, lo, three men stood by him".
Abraham runs to meet them and bows. He fetches water for their feet, has bread baked and a calf prepared, and stands by them under a tree while they eat.
The strangers carry a message from God: Sarah, old and childless, will have a son. Christians have read this visit in more than one way. Some see God with two angels.

Preachers East and West, and later icon painters, came to see in the three a glimpse of the Trinity: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Other pictures of this story show the whole meal, with Abraham and Sarah serving.

teach.h: ONLY THE THREE, SHARING ONE CUP.
teach.b: He paints only the three, at rest, turned toward one another: no old man with a beard for the Father, but three of the same, sharing one cup. In Orthodox prayer an icon isn't decoration.
People pray before it, and some call it a window.

Some viewers say the open place is for whoever stands looking. The circle isn't closed. Hebrews puts the old story to work: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares."
Abraham opened his tent. The icon, some say, opens the table.

how: Orthodox Christians pray before icons such as Rublev's Trinity at home and in church, and copies of it hang in some churches, Orthodox and others, as a picture of the Trinity and of welcome.

o: an icon of three visitors at one cup, with room left open
a Russian church crowned with three golden domes
a hymn about Father, Son and Spirit sung at Easter

p: at the center of the table
the open place for the viewer

s: Rublev painted Abraham and Sarah serving the meal
the icon leaves them out and shows only the three visitors.
Christians read Abraham's visitors in more than one way
some see God with two angels; preachers East and West, and icon painters, came to see a glimpse of the Trinity.
Orthodox Christians treat icons as decoration
they pray in front of them, and some call an icon a window.

games.q: you're Abraham, sitting at your tent door in the heat of the day. three strangers are standing nearby. what do you do?
o: stay in the shade and let them pass.
run to meet them, bow, and bring water and bread.
ask who they are before offering anything.
games.why: Abraham runs, bows, and has water, bread and a meal brought out. only afterward do they bring a message from God.

practice: If you can, pull up a picture of Rublev's Trinity; if not, use the one from the hook, three at a table, one cup, a gap at the front. Let your eyes move slowly around the circle, face to face, then rest on the open side nearest you.
If you pray, pray there, at the edge of the table; if not, notice what it's like to be left room.

wordCard.voice: Rublev's Trinity. An icon of Abraham's three visitors, at rest around one cup, which Christians, especially in the East, read as a picture of the Trinity, with a place at the table left open.

orig.note: Russian: Trinity, the name the icon is known by.

carryVoice: Your line: the open place. Room for one more. See you at the table tomorrow.
